raw.answer: The case asked whether people who share a criminal intent but do not personally carry out the core criminal act can still be treated as joint principal offenders. The court decided that they can, if they took part in other acts with their own shared criminal intent, or planned the crime in advance while others carried it out.
raw.held: Anyone who, with their own intent to commit the crime together, takes part in acts outside the defined elements of the offense, or plans it beforehand while only some of the group carry it out, is a joint principal offender. Three earlier Judicial Yuan interpretations (Nos. 1905, 2030-1 and 2202 first part) are consistent with this.

points.text: Joint principal offenders each take a part of the crime within their shared intent and use one another's acts to reach the criminal goal.
Being a joint principal offender does not require everyone to carry out the defined elements of the offense.
People who join in other acts with shared intent, or plan in advance while only some carry out the crime, are also joint principal offenders and answer for the whole result.

Earlier interpretation 1905 covered planning beforehand and receiving a share of the loot afterward, with others doing the act; 2030-1 covered planning beforehand and acting as lookout; both remain joint principal offenders.
Interpretation 2202 (first part) on a police sergeant colluding with a thief: if he acted with his own criminal intent and took part in carrying it out, he is a joint principal in theft.
The three earlier interpretations use different wording because the requests differed, but their meaning is the same.

who: People who plan a crime but do not carry it out
People who take part in a crime outside its core elements, such as lookouts

raw.answer: The case asked how to count the Constitution's requirement that a person arrested on suspicion of a crime be sent to a court within 24 hours. The court decided that the 24 hours does not include unavoidable delays, such as transport problems or other force majeure, or the necessary travel time to deliver the person. There must still be no unnecessary delay, and the ordinary court rules for deducting travel time do not apply.
raw.held: The 24-hour limit in Article 8, paragraph 2 of the Constitution excludes unavoidable delay from transport obstacles or force majeure, and travel time for escorting the person. There must be no unnecessary delay, and the litigation-law rules on deducting travel time do not apply.

points.text: Article 8, paragraph 2 requires arrested suspects to be sent to court within 24 hours, which protects personal liberty and sets a very strict limit.

In reality, necessary travel takes time, and transport obstacles or other force majeure can cause unavoidable delay. Counting all of that within 24 hours is impossible and was not the framers' intent, so such time is excluded.
Even so, there must be no unnecessary delay, and the person should arrive as quickly as possible, consistent with the Constitution's aim of protecting personal liberty.

The civil and criminal procedure rules on deducting travel time exist to help people performing procedural acts within legal deadlines when they live or work away from the court. Their nature and purpose differ from the constitutional provision, so they do not apply.

who: People arrested on suspicion of a crime

raw.answer: The case was about land expropriation compensation: whether a land authority could throw out its own announced land value and send it to a review committee when no one had objected, and how deadlines for paying compensation work. The court said the authority cannot do that when neither the land user nor the owner objected, and it set rules on the payment deadline, including after a committee re-evaluation.
raw.held: If neither the party needing the land nor the owner objects to the compensation amount, the land authority may not cancel the announced value and send it to the Standard Land Price Review Committee. The 15-day payment deadline still applies, with exceptions for a pending review or owner-approved extension, and after a committee decision payment must be made within a time limit of no more than 15 days.

points.text: Under the cited Land Act articles, the authority estimates compensation where no legal land value exists, and review by the committee happens only when someone objects. So with no objection, the authority has no power to cancel the announced value and send it for re-evaluation.

Under the earlier interpretation cited, approval of an expropriation lapses if payment is not made within 15 days of announcement. But if there was an objection and the matter was properly sent to the committee, or the owner agreed to a delay on record, the owner's interests are not harmed, so approval does not lapse.
The Land Act's payment deadline aims to prevent expropriation approvals from hanging unresolved and to reduce harm to owners and protect their private rights.

The law sets no deadline for paying a value re-evaluated by the committee, but for the same reasons the authority must promptly notify the land user and set a deadline for payment, which may not exceed 15 days.

who: Land owners whose land is expropriated

raw.answer: The case asked whether the right of an owner of registered real estate to demand its return can expire through the passage of time (extinctive prescription). The court decided that it cannot, because the Civil Code's rule on extinctive prescription does not apply to such owners.
raw.held: The right of an owner of registered real estate to demand recovery of the property is not subject to the extinctive prescription rule in Article 125 of the Civil Code.

points.text: The Civil Code lets someone occupying unregistered real estate ask to be registered as owner, but has no similar rule for registered real estate, so registered property is not subject to acquisition by prescription. To match this, the owner's recovery right should not be subject to extinctive prescription under Article 125.

Under Civil Code Article 758 and Land Act Article 43, registration is needed for property rights to take effect and has absolute effect. If the recovery right could expire through time, the registration system would lose its purpose.

A registered owner is named in the register and must pay taxes, while the occupier cannot acquire ownership by prescription. If the owner also lost the recovery right through prescription, the owner would bear duties forever, which would be plainly unfair.
The earlier Interpretation Yuan-tzu No. 1833 addressed owners of unregistered real estate, so this ruling supplements it for registered real estate.

raw.answer: The case asked whether business tax evaded before the business tax law was revised and took effect on December 30, 1965 (ROC year 54) could still be collected under the new rule. The court decided that for such earlier evasion, the five-year limit counts from the date the revised law took effect, and if the evasion is not found within five years of that date, the tax can no longer be collected.
raw.held: When a business hid its sales and evaded business tax before the revised business tax law took effect on December 30, 1965, and the evasion is not discovered within five years counting from that date, the tax may not be collected afterward.

points.text: Article 41 of the business tax law, added when the old law was fully revised in 1965, says that hidden sales not discovered within five years of the event can no longer be taxed.
The law in force before had no time limit, so evasion that happened before the new article could be taxed no matter how much time had passed.
Evasion after the new article is barred after five years undiscovered, so older evasion hidden for many years would still be taxed while newer evasion hidden for only five years would not.
The court found this unfair and not in line with the purpose behind adding Article 41.
So for earlier evasion, the five years should count from the effective date of the revised law, to be fair.

who: Businesses accused of hiding sales to evade business tax

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Publication Act's rules letting administrative agencies suspend a publication for a set period or cancel its registration are constitutional. The court decided they are not unconstitutional. It treated them as necessary limits on freedom of publication.
raw.held: The suspension or registration-cancellation penalties in Articles 40 and 41 of the Publication Act are necessary restrictions under Article 23 of the Constitution. Having administrative agencies handle them directly to carry out the restriction is hard to regard as unconstitutional.

points.text: The penalties in Articles 40 and 41 are restrictions on freedom of publication made under the necessary circumstances in Article 23 of the Constitution, a view the request for interpretation also shared.
The Constitution places no limit on how illegal publications may be dealt with, so using administrative penalties to carry out the restriction is hard to call unconstitutional.
The conditions for imposing penalties are very strict, and agencies may act only on the conditions listed in those articles.
A person penalized can file an administrative appeal and bring an administrative court action to seek relief, which gives enough protection.

who: Publishers of periodicals and other publications
Administrative agencies enforcing the Publication Act

raw.answer: The case asked how income tax should be withheld on interest that arises when foreign suppliers are paid in installments. The court decided that when installment payments to a foreign firm carry interest, the party paying must still withhold the tax on that interest at the time of payment.
raw.held: If installment payments to a foreign firm include interest, the interest income is still subject to tax withholding by the withholding agent when the payment is made.

points.text: Under Article 86, item 3 of the Income Tax Act (in force from 1 January 1956), the taxpayer on interest is the person who receives it. This is not limited to natural persons, and businesses that receive interest are not an exception.
Under Article 85, paragraph 1 of the same Act, the withholding agent must still withhold the tax. The obligation does not go away because the recipient of the interest is not a natural person.
So for installment payments to foreign firms that carry interest, the withholding agent must withhold on the interest when paying.

who: Withholding agents who pay foreign firms
Foreign firms paid in installments with interest

raw.answer: The case asked whether a court must record a fine-conversion rate when a sentence for one crime, which could normally be served by paying a fine, is combined with a sentence for a crime that cannot be converted. The court decided that no such rate needs to be recorded for the part that could otherwise have been converted.
raw.held: When one of several combined crimes could normally be converted to a fine but, because it is combined with a non-convertible crime, can no longer be converted, the sentence for the convertible part does not need to state a fine-conversion standard.

points.text: Under Article 41 of the Criminal Code, a fine-conversion standard is recorded only for crimes with a maximum penalty of three years or less, where the sentence is six months or less in prison or detention.

When crimes are combined and one is non-convertible, the court just weighs the sentences together and sets an executed sentence that cannot be converted to a fine, so Article 309, item 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not apply.
An earlier interpretation (院字第2702號) already said no conversion standard need be recorded, and this covers not just the combined sentence but also the part that could originally have been converted.
A court that, after a combined judgment is final, separately orders fine conversion for one part by ruling has that ruling treated as invalid.

If the other crime is later found not guilty on appeal or is pardoned, the remaining convertible crime may be converted if serving the sentence would be truly difficult because of the defendant's body, education, occupation or family. The defendant and prosecutor can both apply, and the court may then rule appropriately.

who: Defendants convicted of several crimes at once

raw.answer: The case asked whether an enforcement fee can be charged when a provisional seizure or provisional disposition is carried out, given that a fee is charged again when the final judgment is enforced. The court decided the fee may be charged at the provisional stage, and the amount is deducted when the fee is charged for enforcing the final judgment. It also changed an earlier interpretation (院解字第三九九一號) that had said no such fee was needed.
raw.held: Carrying out a provisional seizure or provisional disposition may be charged an enforcement fee under Article 23 of the Civil Litigation Costs Act, and that fee is deducted when the enforcement fee is charged once the main case is final. The earlier interpretation, 院解字第三九九一號, is changed.

points.text: Provisional seizure and provisional disposition are kinds of civil compulsory enforcement, so the fee rule in Article 23 of the Civil Litigation Costs Act applies to them too.

The earlier interpretation said no fee was needed because a fee would be charged anyway when the final judgment or settlement is enforced, so there was no need to charge first at the preservation stage.
But if the applicant later does not seek enforcement on the main judgment, or the main suit is dismissed, there would be no chance to charge the fee, which does not fit the article.
So it is fairer to order payment during the preservation enforcement and deduct it when the fee is charged on enforcement of the final main case; the earlier interpretation is changed to that extent.

who: People who apply for provisional seizure or provisional disposition

raw.answer: The case asked whether a court order correcting a criminal judgment, as allowed under the court's earlier Interpretation No. 43, must involve the judges who made the original judgment. The court decided it does not. It reasoned that such corrections only fix obvious writing mistakes and do not change the substance of the judgment.
raw.held: A correction order under Interpretation No. 43 does not require the participation of the judges who made the original judgment.

points.text: Interpretation No. 43 allows correction by order only of criminal judgments where the wording is clearly a writing mistake.
Such a correction does not affect the overall facts of the case or the main purpose of the judgment, so the original judges need not take part.

who: Judges who made the original judgment
People whose criminal judgments contain writing errors

raw.answer: The case asked whether the time limit for carrying out a sentence stops running when a convict whose sentence is being carried out is wanted by warrant and the sentence cannot start or continue. The court said yes, the limit stops running, though a limit in Article 85, paragraph 3 of the Criminal Code must still be kept in mind. It also confirmed that the time limit for prosecuting a defendant on trial who is wanted by warrant stops running.
raw.held: The time limit for prosecuting a defendant on trial who is lawfully wanted stops running, and an earlier interpretation (院字第一九六三號) is unchanged. The time limit for carrying out a sentence also stops running when a convict is lawfully wanted and the sentence cannot start or continue, subject to Article 85, paragraph 3 of the Criminal Code.

points.text: A trial cannot go on if the defendant is absent, and a defendant who flees or hides may be made the subject of a wanted warrant.

When a defendant on trial flees or hides and is lawfully wanted, the trial cannot start or continue, so the prosecution time limit should stop running, subject to Article 83, paragraph 3 of the Criminal Code.
The earlier interpretation (院字第一九六三號, item 1) on this point has not been changed.
To compel a convict to appear, a wanted warrant may be issued, as shown by the Code of Criminal Procedure provisions on carrying out sentences.
When a convict flees or hides, is lawfully wanted, and the sentence cannot start or continue, the time limit for carrying out the sentence stops running under Article 85, paragraph 1.

If the stopping cause lasts to one quarter of the periods in Article 84, paragraph 1, it is treated as ended; if the sentence is still not carried out and there is no other cause for stopping, the time limit resumes.

who: Defendants on trial who are wanted by warrant
Convicts serving or about to serve sentences who are wanted by warrant

raw.answer: The case asked whether a civil servant who was suspended from duty before a disciplinary decision can still return to the job when a period of demotion-style leave (休職) ends. The court decided that the earlier suspension does not block that return. The rule on returning after the leave period still applies.
raw.held: The return to duty after the leave period ends, under Article 4, paragraph 2 of the Civil Servants Discipline Act, is not excluded just because the person was suspended before the disciplinary decision.

points.text: The two kinds of return are different in nature. One under Article 16, paragraph 3 restores the post from which the person was suspended before the decision. The other under Article 4, paragraph 2 restores the post after the leave punishment has been carried out.
Article 4, paragraph 2 expressly allows a return when the leave period ends.
So anyone given the leave punishment is not shut out of that rule because they were suspended before the decision.

who: Civil servants given a leave (休職) punishment
Civil servants suspended before a disciplinary decision

raw.answer: The case asked whether a criminal judgment is unlawful just because the court never served the defendant with a copy of the private prosecution complaint, even though the defendant knew the charges and took part in the hearing. The court decided that it is not unlawful in that situation. It also clarified an earlier interpretation (院字第一三二０號, part 2).
raw.held: A private prosecution complaint must be filed with copies for each defendant, and if copies are missing but can be fixed, the court orders them supplied within a deadline. If the defendant was told the content of the charges and a lawful oral hearing took place, the judgment cannot be called unlawful just because the copy was not served.

points.text: The complaint must come with copies for each defendant, as the Code of Criminal Procedure states.
If copies are missing but this can be corrected, the court orders correction by a deadline. If the complainant deliberately refuses, the court must dismiss the case without hearing it on the merits.
Serving the copy on the defendant is the court's duty, and the court should do it promptly, but the law allows an exception where summoning or arresting the defendant first is needed.
If the defendant was told what the charges were and a lawful oral hearing was held before judgment, non-service of the copy cannot make the judgment unlawful.
So the earlier interpretation (院字第一三二０號, part 2) is supplemented and clarified.

raw.answer: The question was whether the time limit for prosecuting a crime keeps running while a case is already in trial after a public prosecution or private prosecution has been filed. The court decided that it does not, because the right to prosecute is being exercised during that time. The ruling treats the time limit as running only when the right to prosecute is not exercised.
raw.held: Once a case has been brought by public or private prosecution and is being tried, the right to prosecute is not going unused, so no question of the time limit running arises.

points.text: Under Article 80, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code, the right to prosecute expires only if it is not exercised within the stated periods. So the time limit runs because of non-exercise, and where it is exercised there is no running of time.
Filing a public or private prosecution, and carrying out the prosecution during the trial, all count as exercising the right to prosecute.
The cases in question are ones where the right to prosecute has not expired and is currently being exercised under the law, so there is no non-exercise and the time limit does not run.

Where the right to prosecute legally cannot be exercised, Article 83 of the Criminal Code separately provides for the time limit to be suspended. The earlier interpretations rested on that article and were not changed, and they do not address whether time runs while the right is being exercised.

who: People being prosecuted in a criminal case

raw.answer: The case asked whether a government office may jump straight to direct compulsory measures when a person keeps ignoring a duty after being fined again and again. The court decided it may not, because repeated fines mean indirect measures are still possible under the Administrative Execution Act.
raw.held: When an authority has repeatedly fined someone for not meeting a duty under Article 4 of the Administrative Execution Act and the person still does not comply, this is not a case where indirect measures are impossible under Article 11, so the authority cannot go straight to direct compulsory measures.

points.text: Having repeatedly imposed fines under the law, the authority cannot say indirect measures are impossible, so the situation is not the one described in Article 11 of the Act.
If the person still does not comply, the authority should instruct and warn them and keep imposing fines to push them to perform the duty.
The authority therefore cannot suddenly apply direct compulsory measures.

who: People with duties to act or refrain from acting under Article 4 of the Administrative Execution Act
People repeatedly fined who still do not comply

raw.answer: The question was whether buying train tickets in order to resell them at a profit counts as fraud. The court decided there is no blanket answer: it depends on whether the buyer actually used deceit that led the ticket office into a mistake and met every element of fraud.
raw.held: Whether ticket resale for profit is fraud depends on whether the actual facts show deceit that misled the ticket office and satisfy all the elements of fraud. The two earlier interpretations (2920 and 3808) refer to purchases using deceit, and they apply under paragraphs 1 and 2 of Article 339 of the Criminal Code respectively.

points.text: Fraud requires that the facts actually show deceit causing a mistake and meet all the elements of the offense, so each case is judged on its specific facts.

Where someone who does not intend to ride mixes in with passengers and buys tickets to resell at a high price, it still must be shown that deceit misled the ticket office; ticket types and purchase limits vary in strictness.
If elements of fraud are missing, the conduct cannot readily be punished as fraud even if other laws may justify restricting or banning it.
The word 'bulk purchasing' (套購) in the earlier interpretations means a purchase that uses deceit.

The later interpretation (3808) focuses on deceiving passengers into handing over property, so Article 339 paragraph 1 applies; the earlier one (2920) focuses on deceiving the ticket office to gain unlawful benefit, so paragraph 2 applies.

raw.answer: The case asked how a lease made under the Cultivated Land 37.5% Rent Reduction Act can be ended before its term runs out. The court decided that Article 17 of that Act alone sets out when this can happen, so the termination rules in the Land Act and the Civil Code do not apply.
raw.held: A lease made under the Act may be ended early only in the situations listed in Article 17 of the Act. Article 114 of the Land Act and Article 438 of the Civil Code on ending leases do not apply.

points.text: Both the Land Act and the Civil Code have rules on ending farmland leases, but Article 17 of the Act expressly says that before the term ends a lease may not be ended unless one of the listed situations exists.
So a landlord may end the lease only in a situation listed in that article, which the ruling calls clear from its wording.
Under the first part of Article 1 of the Act, there is no room to apply Land Act Article 114 or Civil Code Article 438 to end the lease.
If a tenant breaks those Civil Code and Land Act rules, the landlord may seek restoration or damages, or claim the lease is void under Article 16, paragraph 2 of the Act. These are separate matters.

who: Tenant farmers under 37.5% rent reduction leases

raw.answer: The case was about who must pay court fees that were never paid, or not paid in full, on the first appeal, when a party appeals a retrial judgment. The court decided that the court must first collect the shortfall from the first appellant. If it is still unpaid once the judgment can be enforced, the court sets the amount by order and has the party bearing the litigation costs pay it.
raw.held: When a retrial judgment is appealed and the court fees for the first appeal are unpaid or short, the court must collect them from the first appellant. If they remain unpaid after the judgment becomes enforceable, the court must on its own set the amount by order and have the party bearing the litigation costs pay it. This supplements the earlier Interpretation Yuan-Jie No. 2936 (2) on court fees.

points.text: Court fees are a fee the state is supposed to collect, and courts must set them according to the value of what the case is about, so parties cannot underpay or skip them. This fits the principle of paid litigation in the Code of Civil Procedure.
The earlier interpretation said a court cannot order the first appellant to make up a shortfall in first-appeal fees on an appeal from a retrial judgment.
That earlier statement only means the court may not re-examine whether the first appeal met its requirements. It does not mean the fees need not be fully collected.

So the court must collect unpaid or short fees from the first appellant. If they are still unpaid once the judgment is enforceable, the court sets the amount by order on its own and has the party bearing the costs pay it.

who: First appellants who underpaid court fees
Parties ordered to bear litigation costs
Courts handling appeals of retrial judgments

raw.answer: The case asked whether a person who deposited money or goods with a court to pay off a debt, and later takes it back, is covered by an earlier ruling (No. 39) on deposits. The court said that earlier ruling does not cover this kind of deposit made for a creditor under Article 326 of the Civil Code. But if the depositor is legally allowed to take the deposit back, Article 125 of the Civil Code still applies.
raw.held: The deposits meant in Interpretation No. 39 do not include a debtor's payment deposit made for a creditor under Civil Code Article 326. Where such a depositor may legally take back the deposit, Civil Code Article 125 still applies.

points.text: Interpretation No. 39 was meant to clarify an earlier interpretation (院解字第3239號), and its wording on returning case funds and taking back deposits refers only to custody deposits, not payment deposits for a creditor under Article 326.
The earlier interpretation's wording about returning bail money and civil court funds held by the court makes this reading even clearer.
Where a payment depositor can take back the deposit under Articles 11 or 13 of the Deposit Act, that Act sets no special time limit for the claim, so Civil Code Article 125 applies.

The agency's question about notice after a payment deposit and the ten-year period under Article 330 was not treated as a real doubt about Interpretation No. 39, since it does not differ from a Supreme Court precedent, so no interpretation was given on it.

who: Persons entitled to take back deposits

raw.answer: The question was what remedy exists when a criminal judgment has become final and it is later found that the facts the court found clearly do not match the evidence it relied on. The court decided that this counts as a trial that violated the law, so an extraordinary appeal can be filed. If there is also a ground for retrial, a retrial can still be requested.
raw.held: A final criminal judgment whose found facts clearly do not match the evidence it used is a trial that violated the law, and can be challenged by extraordinary appeal. If a ground for retrial exists, a retrial can still be requested.

points.text: Where the found facts clearly conflict with the evidence used, it is a trial that violated the law, so an extraordinary appeal may be filed.
If the mismatch is only a writing error that does not affect the overall case or the judgment's meaning, it can be corrected under Interpretation No. 43 instead.

The extraordinary appeal court applies Article 445, paragraph 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which applies Article 394, and works from the facts the original judgment confirmed, to correct the legal error.
If the violation affected how the facts were determined and a ground for retrial exists, a retrial can still be requested through the retrial procedure.

who: People convicted in final criminal judgments
Courts handling extraordinary appeals and retrials

raw.answer: The case asked whether a co-owner of a house and land can mortgage his or her share. The court said that where the property is co-owned other than through a 'joint ownership' (公同關係) relationship, each co-owner may mortgage his or her own share. The ruling does not directly answer the question as framed about joint-ownership property beyond saying the rule applies to non-joint co-ownership.
raw.held: For co-owned houses and land that are not co-owned through a joint-ownership relationship, each co-owner may set a mortgage on his or her own share.

points.text: Article 819, paragraph 1 of the Civil Code says each co-owner may freely dispose of his or her own share.

Where the co-owned property is real estate, and a need arises to give security without handing over possession, a co-owner may therefore mortgage his or her share. This is subject to any different rules for joint-ownership cases.
Article 819, paragraph 2 requires all co-owners' consent to dispose of, change, or encumber the co-owned property itself, but this refers to the property as a whole, not to each person's share.
Comparing with paragraph 1's free disposal rule, the meaning of the law is very clear; the court's earlier Interpretation Yuan-zi No. 1516 is to be supplemented and clarified.

who: Co-owners who are not in a joint-ownership relationship
Creditors taking a mortgage on a co-owner's share

raw.answer: The case asked under what conditions a farmland tenant can use the right of first refusal when the land is sold or pledged out. The court decided that the tenant's right only comes into play once the landlord gives the tenant written notice of the sale or pledge terms. A tenant's earlier statement giving up the right does not change this.
raw.held: Under Article 15, paragraph 1 of the Farmland 37.5% Rent Reduction Act, the tenant may accept or waive only after the landlord notifies the tenant in writing of the sale or pledge terms. A tenant's advance waiver does not exclude this rule.

points.text: The rule is rooted in the constitutional policy of supporting owner-farmers, giving tenants first right to take the land on the sale or pledge terms of the time.
Notice of the terms must be in writing, to protect the tenant's interests.
The right of first refusal arises only when the land is actually sold or pledged out, and the tenant can accept or waive only after receiving written notice of the terms.
A waiver made in advance, whether to the landlord or to other tenants, comes when there are no sale terms and no sale, so the legal right has not yet arisen and cannot have been lost.
When land is later sold or pledged, the landlord must still give written notice, and only a failure to accept in writing within fifteen days counts as waiver.

raw.answer: The case asked what "many people" (多數人) means in the court's earlier Interpretation No. 2033, which said that "publicly" (公然) in the criminal code's specific offenses covers situations that unspecified people or many people can see or hear. The court clarified that "many people" includes a specific, identified group of many people. How many people are needed depends on the purpose of the law and on whether the real situation reached the level of being public.
raw.held: The court held that "many people" in Interpretation No. 2033 includes a specific group of many people. The number needed depends on the legislative purpose and on whether the actual circumstances amount to being public.

points.text: Interpretation 2033 said "publicly" only requires a situation where unspecified people or many people can see or hear together, so people need not actually have seen or heard. But in fact there must be a situation in which they could.
The court said "many people" includes a specific group of many people, as the earlier interpretation and the original request for it make clear.
Counting a specific group depends on the legislative purpose and actual circumstances, because the elements and nature of each offense differ.

who: People involved in cases where "publicly" (公然) is an element of an offense

raw.answer: The case asked whether a person who joined a rebel organization before turning 14 can be held criminally responsible. The court decided that if the person had not turned themselves in by age 14 and nothing else shows they had left, they must bear criminal responsibility.
raw.held: A person who joined a rebel organization before age 14 and, on turning 14, had not turned themselves in and has no other proven departure, must bear criminal responsibility. Interpretation No. 68 also applies.

points.text: The Criminal Code Article 18, paragraph 1 expressly says acts of people under 14 are not punished.
Joining a rebel organization is an ongoing act, so it continues after the person turns 14 if they have not left.
Because the act is still continuing at 14, with no self-surrender or other proof of leaving, the person must bear criminal responsibility, and Interpretation No. 68 applies.
Whether grounds for exemption or reduction of punishment exist is a factual question for the proper authority, outside the scope of this interpretation.

who: People who joined a rebel organization before age 14
People who reach 14 still in a rebel organization
Authorities deciding exemption or reduction of punishment

raw.answer: The case asked how much one day counts for when a criminal fine is converted (易科罰金) or when a person works off a fine as labor service (易服勞役). The court decided that, if the original amount is raised two-fold under the special 戡亂時期 raising-standards act, one day is calculated at 3, 6 or 9 yuan. Courts must pick one of those three figures.
raw.held: If the original per-day amount is raised two-fold under the 戡亂時期罰金罰鍰裁判費執行費公證費提高標準條例, one day is converted at 3, 6 or 9 yuan.

points.text: The original range of 'one yuan or more, three yuan or less' means exactly 1, 2 or 3 yuan per day. The ruling says this is clear from the Criminal Code's provisions that a fine is at least one yuan and that amounts under one yuan from increasing or reducing a sentence are not counted.
Once the competent authority raised the amount two-fold under Articles 2 and 4 of the raising-standards act, the figures become 3, 6 or 9 yuan.
In trial, a court must choose one of those three amounts. It may not set any other amount between 3 and 9 yuan that is not the original amount raised two-fold.
The proportional conversion rule in Article 42, paragraph 3 of the Criminal Code is for exceptional situations and should not be confused with this rule.

who: People who can convert a fine or work it off as labor service
Courts setting the daily conversion amount

raw.answer: The case asked whether a company's articles of incorporation can require more shareholders to attend a meeting, or more voting power, than the minimum set by the Company Act. The court decided that they can. The legal figures are only minimums, and setting higher ones is not forbidden.
raw.held: The attendance and voting figures in the cited Company Act provisions are minimums. A company may set higher attendance and voting requirements in its articles, and the law does not forbid it.

points.text: One provision requires a shareholder meeting resolution to have shareholders representing at least two-thirds of total shares present, and approval by a majority of those present.
Another provision requires shareholders representing at least three-fourths of total shares present, and approval by a majority of the voting rights of those present.
Both provisions set only a lowest limit on attendance and voting rights. Neither limits raising that minimum.
So a company whose articles set higher attendance and voting requirements than the legal minimum is not doing something the law prohibits.

who: Companies and their articles of incorporation

raw.answer: The case asked whether certain rules in a supplementary regulation on filling vacant seats of First National Assembly delegates conflict with the Constitution. The rules treat a delegate whose whereabouts have been unknown for three or more years, and who did not report in person within the government's announced deadline, as having left the seat. The court decided these rules do not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 3, item 1 and Article 4 of the supplementary regulation on filling vacancies among First National Assembly delegates do not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The Constitution says the election and removal of National Assembly delegates are to be set by law.
The supplementary regulation adds to the existing election and removal law for delegates and its enforcement rules.

Article 3, item 1 treats a delegate missing for three or more years who did not report in person to the designated office by the announced deadline as having left the seat. Article 4 makes a reserve candidate in that situation lose candidate status.
These rules were created to meet the nation's needs after the central government moved to Taiwan, and they do not conflict with the relevant constitutional provisions.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a member of the Control Yuan (a supervisory official) may also work as the publisher of a newspaper or magazine. The court decided that a publisher's work falls within the "business" that Article 103 of the Constitution bars these officials from doing.
raw.held: The work done by publishers of newspapers and magazines belongs within the scope of the "business" mentioned in Article 103 of the Constitution.

points.text: Control Yuan members hold a supervisory post and are meant to stand in an impartial position, which is why Article 103 bars them from doing business.
Publishing a newspaper or magazine needs approval from an administrative authority, and publishers' work is supervised by that authority.
Because of this, the publisher's work is plainly incompatible with the supervisory powers of a Control Yuan member, so it falls within the business covered by Article 103.

raw.answer: The case asked whether directors of state-run enterprises who represent private shareholders are covered by the Civil Servants Service Act when they are paid. The court said the earlier Interpretation No. 92 meant only those who receive a salary. Directors and supervisors who receive no salary are not covered.
raw.held: The Civil Servants Service Act applies to directors and supervisors representing private shares in public enterprises only if they receive a salary (俸給). Interpretation No. 92 is clarified accordingly.

points.text: Directors and supervisors representing private shares in a public enterprise are service personnel of that enterprise, so under Article 24 of the Civil Servants Service Act the Act should apply to them.
However, that article is limited to service personnel of public enterprises who receive a salary, so those representing private shares who receive no salary are not covered by the Act.
For this reason, Interpretation No. 92 needed to be supplemented and explained, and it was read as referring to salaried people.

who: Directors of public enterprises representing private shares
Supervisors of public enterprises representing private shares

raw.answer: The case asked whether the chairman and general manager of a shipping company are criminally liable for professional negligence when a ship suffers a disaster at sea after the company issued a sailing notice. The court decided they are not automatically liable just because the notice was issued. They can be liable if their own negligence in urging the ship to sail caused the disaster.
raw.held: Issuing a sailing notice does not by itself make a shipping company's chairman or general manager criminally liable for professional negligence if the ship has a disaster. The exception is where they negligently pushed the ship to sail and that caused the harm.

points.text: The Maritime Law says only the ship's captain is responsible for commanding the ship.
Because the captain is employed by the company, he is still subject to the company's direction and supervision within the scope of his work.
Seamen's service rules require a sailing or moving notice from the company or its agent before a ship may sail or move.
The sailing notice only tells the ship it may sail, so issuing it in the course of their duties does not by itself make the chairman or general manager liable if a disaster follows.
Liability remains where their negligence in urging the ship to sail caused the disaster.

raw.answer: The case was about how to work out the taxable price (the 完稅價格) of goods newly subject to the goods tax, in particular whether freight can be deducted. The court decided that where the goods have a market wholesale price, the taxable price is the factory price without tax or freight. Where there is no market wholesale price and the manufacturer's own freight is already included in the factory price, that freight cannot be deducted.
raw.held: Where new-tax goods have a market wholesale price, the taxable price is the factory price that includes no tax or freight. Where there is no wholesale price and the manufacturer's own freight is already in the factory price, that freight may not be deducted when calculating the tax.

points.text: The Goods Tax Act, Article 8, says that when the market wholesale price of new-tax goods does not yet include tax, the factory price may temporarily serve as the taxable price.
The factory price by definition does not include tax or freight, as Article 3, item 1(4) of the same Act provides.
Freight paid by the manufacturer itself and included in the factory price of goods with no wholesale price differs from freight paid by wholesalers within a market wholesale price.
Because of this difference, the manufacturer's freight cannot be deducted from the taxable price.

raw.answer: The case asked how far an earlier interpretation (院解字第3827號) on applying for retirement or being ordered to retire reaches. The court decided it applies only to events that happened while the 1943 civil servants retirement law was in force.
raw.held: The earlier interpretation's reference to applying for or being ordered to retire applies only to events that occurred while the civil servants retirement law promulgated in 1943 (year 32 of the Republic) was in effect.

points.text: The earlier interpretation explained the meaning of 'retirement from service' in Article 11 of the civil servants retirement law promulgated and enforced in 1943.
The law's content was later changed several times, so the interpretation only applies to events during the period that law was valid.

Where an event during that law's enforcement fits applying for or being ordered to retire, a retirement payment may be claimed on that basis, unless five years have passed since the month after resignation approval, dismissal or discharge.

who: Civil servants who retired or were ordered to retire under the 1943 law

raw.answer: A resident challenged the Interior Ministry's approval of a Taipei City urban plan change that turned residential land into government-use land for an asphalt concrete plant. The Administrative Court dismissed the suit on procedural grounds, saying a plan change is not an administrative act aimed at a specific person. The Constitutional Court held that even if that dismissal conflicted with an earlier court precedent, it does not raise the question of whether a law or order applied in a final judgment is unconstitutional.
raw.held: If the Administrative Court dismisses a suit over an urban plan change by ruling that it is not an administrative act toward a specific person, then even if the ruling conflicts with the court's own precedent, it does not raise a constitutional question about the law or order applied in a final judgment.

points.text: The Administrative Court regarded an authority's urban plan change as not an administrative act directed at a specific person, so people could not sue over it, and it dismissed the case on procedural grounds without examining the merits.
Even if that dismissal did not match the court's 1959 precedent (判字第192號), that mismatch only concerns whether a retrial can be requested by law as a remedy.
Therefore it does not raise the question of whether a law or order applied in a final, conclusive judgment conflicts with the Constitution.

raw.answer: The case asked what "世所共知" (commonly known throughout the world) means in Article 2, item 8 of the Trademark Act. The court decided that it means something generally well known within the territory of the Republic of China. It reasoned that the Trademark Act is national legislation whose effect covers the whole country.
raw.held: The phrase "世所共知" in Article 2, item 8 of the Trademark Act refers to what is generally known within the territory of the Republic of China.

points.text: The Trademark Act is central legislation that applies across the whole country, and trademark registration is effective nationwide.
Each paragraph of Article 3 of the same Act refers to the territory of the Republic of China, which shows the Act's territorial scope.

So the phrase in Article 2, item 8 means generally known within the Republic of China, and the court's earlier Interpretation (院字) No. 1008, item 2, which concerned item 6 of the pre-amendment Article 2, is clarified accordingly.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the rules for managing 雇員 (junior government employees) should follow the Civil Service Service Act (公務員服務法). The court decided that, unless other laws say differently, they should. It also said an earlier interpretation (院解字第二九零三號) that exempted these employees from Article 13, paragraph 1 of that Act no longer applies.
raw.held: The management of 雇員 follows the provisions of the 公務員服務法 unless laws or orders provide otherwise. The earlier interpretation exempting them from Article 13, paragraph 1 no longer applies.

points.text: 雇員 are not the salaried civil or military officials named in Article 24 of the Act, but they are still people who perform public duties under the law.
Article 21, paragraph 2 of the 公務人員任用法 says the Examination Yuan sets the 雇員 management rules.
Article 13 (latter part) of the Examination Yuan's 雇員 management rules says the Act's provisions apply to 雇員, so their management should follow the Act unless other rules say otherwise.
The earlier interpretation was made in June 1945 under the laws then in force. Those laws have since changed, so its exemption from Article 13, paragraph 1 no longer applies.

who: Public officials covered by the 公務員服務法

raw.answer: The case asked whether a public servant may also serve as chair or director of a private school. The court decided they may not, unless a law or order specifically allows it. It also said an earlier interpretation (院字第二三二０號) needed to be clarified by this ruling.
raw.held: Public servants covered by the Civil Servants Service Act may not serve as chair or director of a private school, unless a law or order says they may. The earlier interpretation No. 2320 is supplemented and clarified.

points.text: Under the Civil Code provision the ruling cites, a director represents the legal entity externally in all its affairs.

A private school is an educational enterprise responsible for training people, so it differs from entities such as guild halls or charities, and its main matters are decided by the chair and directors.
The chair or director role is therefore hard to describe as something other than the 'business' referred to in Article 14 of the Civil Servants Service Act.

Unless a law or order allows it because of practical need, the ban applies whether or not the school has registered as a legal entity, in line with the Act's purpose of limiting other posts held by public servants.
The school regulations let a public servant who founded a private school serve as a director, which fits the exception in Article 14; other laws or orders may allow it where there is practical need.

who: Public servants under the Civil Servants Service Act
Public servants who founded private schools

raw.answer: The case asked whether a public servant convicted of corruption must be removed from office, even when the sentence was suspended or the offence was found out only after the sentence was served. The court decided that such a person must still be dismissed.
raw.held: Public servants who commit corruption must still be dismissed if the suspended sentence ran out without being revoked, or if they committed another crime and the sentence was fully served before it came to light.

points.text: Under Article 15, item 2 of the Public Service Appointment Act, anyone who has served in public office and committed corruption cannot be a public servant once the judgment is final.

A suspended sentence does not remove the effect of the final judgment, so the person should be dismissed at that time. Even if the offence is found out only after the suspension period ends without revocation, dismissal cannot be avoided.

Other offences also bar or suspend public service: treason-type offences (internal disorder, external aggression) after a final judgment, and detention-or-heavier sentences being served, as set out in the Act and Article 17, item 3 of the Civil Servant Discipline Act.

Because the person was already barred from being a public servant when the judgment became final or the sentence began, the office should be ended. Discovery after the sentence was served should not stop those provisions from applying.

who: Public servants whose crimes were found out after serving the sentence

raw.answer: The case asked what remedy exists when a prosecutor has already brought a case to court and then later issues a decision not to prosecute it anyway. The court decided that such a decision is unlawful. If the person who filed the complaint properly asks for review, the senior prosecutor at the higher level must cancel the original decision.
raw.held: When a prosecutor, after a case is already before a court, unlawfully decides on the merits not to prosecute, and the complainant properly asks for review, the chief prosecutor of the higher court must revoke that original decision.

points.text: Once a case has been filed and is before a court, it must be tried according to law.
A prosecutor's later decision not to prosecute on the merits is a serious violation of the law and is void.
Because the void decision still has formal effect, the higher chief prosecutor should cancel it when the complainant properly seeks review, to correct the error.

raw.answer: The case asked how far Articles 16 and 18 of the National General Mobilization Act reach when the government limits people's exercise of creditor rights and performance of debts. The court decided the government is not restricted to imposing limits on everyone or on all banks, companies and factories. It may also impose them on particular areas or particular situations, and the Executive Yuan's relief order for important enterprises was not found unlawful.
raw.held: The limits allowed by Articles 16 and 18 may be applied to a specific area or situation, not only to everyone. The Executive Yuan's important-enterprise relief order, which applies to all qualifying companies limited by shares, was not found unlawful, but any limit on claims and debts must not go beyond what is necessary to achieve the Act's tasks.

points.text: The two articles do not say the government may only restrict all people or all banks, companies and factories; limits can also target particular areas or particular situations.
The Act's implementation outline also makes this point clear.

The relief order covers important production, public utility or transport companies limited by shares whose products or services are needed domestically or have export markets, that risk stopping work but could be rebuilt. The government may attach limits on their claims and debts when giving relief.
Because every company meeting the order's conditions and type can come under it, the order was not found contrary to law.
How far limits on exercising claims and performing debts may go depends on actual circumstances and has no concrete standard, but the limit is what is necessary to achieve the Act's tasks.

who: Companies limited by shares in important production, public utility or transport businesses
Creditors whose claims may be limited
Debtors whose obligations may be limited
Banks, companies and factories in particular areas or situations

raw.answer: The case asked whether an owner who has already given someone a dian right (a right to pay a price and occupy and use a property) over a property may also create a mortgage on it for another person. The court decided that the owner may, as long as the mortgage does not harm the dian right. It also said its earlier Interpretation No. 192 does not need to be changed.
raw.held: After setting up a dian right on a property, the owner may still create a mortgage on it for another person, provided this does not interfere with the dian right. Yuan Interpretation No. 192 stays unchanged.

points.text: A dian right means paying a price and occupying another's property to use it and take its benefits, while a mortgage does not transfer possession and only secures a debt, so the two are not incompatible in nature.
After creating a dian right the owner has not lost ownership, so within the limit of not harming the dian right the owner can still create a mortgage with someone else.
The property part of the Civil Code has no rule forbidding this, so it cannot be seen as impermissible.

who: Owners of real property with a dian right

raw.answer: The case asked how the speech of local council members at meetings should be protected. The court said the Constitution has no rule on this, and that an earlier interpretation (院解字第三七三五號) does not raise a constitutional problem. The ruling does not set out a detailed protection scheme.
raw.held: The Constitution does not say how local council members' speech at meetings must be protected. The earlier interpretation 院解字第三七三五號 does not raise a constitutional problem.

points.text: The Constitution has no provision on how local council members' speech at meetings should be protected.
The earlier interpretation was issued about county councillors who abused their immunity for speech, so it does not raise a constitutional problem.
Provincial, county and city council members who do not abuse this immunity keep their speech protection unaffected.

who: Provincial, county and city council members
County councillors who abuse speech immunity

raw.answer: The case asked what "exempting the sentence" (免除其刑) means in an earlier interpretation, No. 3534. That interpretation is used to decide who counts as a repeat offender. The court said it means only an exemption that comes from the pardon power reducing a sentence, and not other kinds of sentence exemption.
raw.held: The phrase "exempting the sentence" in Interpretation No. 3534 refers only to a sentence exemption that results from the pardon power reducing a sentence. It does not include other sentence exemptions.

points.text: Under Criminal Code Article 47, a person who commits a new offense within five years after a pardon, following completed or partly served imprisonment, is a repeat offender. The earlier interpretation said "pardon" covers special pardon and sentence exemption but not general amnesty.
The "exemption" in that interpretation means a sentence reduction to nothing that arises from the pardon power.

Other exemptions, such as those in Articles 23, 24(1), 26 and 27 provisos, do not come from the pardon power. Courts impose them through a judgment under the Code of Criminal Procedure that waives punishment.

Those other exemptions involve no prison sentence being served, so they have nothing to do with the elements of repeat-offender status and are not included. The court therefore supplemented its earlier interpretation.

who: People who received a pardon-based sentence exemption
People whose punishment was waived by a court judgment

raw.answer: An owner first set up a mortgage on a piece of real estate and later gave a third party a dian right (典權) over the same property. The question was whether, if the mortgage debt goes unpaid, the dian right can be removed so the property can be auctioned. The court said yes, in certain circumstances: the mortgage is not weakened by the later dian right, and the enforcement court may remove the dian right and auction the property again.
raw.held: A mortgage is not affected by a dian right created later on the same property. If the mortgage debt is unpaid and the auction fails because of the dian right (no buyers, or bids too low to cover the debt), the enforcement court may remove the dian right, re-appraise the property and auction it again.

points.text: The civil code article cited (Article 866) allows an owner to create a dian right after a mortgage, but its proviso says the mortgage is not affected by it.
A later dian right that affects the mortgage has no effect against the mortgage holder.

To balance the interests of the mortgage holder and the dian right holder, the dian right may be removed only if the auction fails because of it, meaning no one bids or bids are too low to cover the debt.
If the sale brings in more than the mortgage debt, the dian right holder's dian price has priority over later-registered rights holders.
When the court issues the certificate of transfer, it must notify the land administration office on its own initiative to cancel the dian right registration.
This ruling supplements the explanation given in the earlier Interpretation Yuan-tzu No. 1446.

raw.answer: The case asked what happens when a higher court wrongly overturns a lower court's judgment and sends the case back for retrial, even though the parties were not allowed to appeal or never filed an objection. The court decided that the higher court's judgment and the later retrial judgment seriously violate the law and have no legal effect. Because they still take the form of judgments, they can be challenged through the usual legal procedures.
raw.held: In civil and criminal cases, a higher court's judgment that wrongly overturns or sends back a lower court's judgment (where appeal was not allowed or was not filed), and the retrial judgment after it, are gravely unlawful and without effect. Since they have the form of a judgment, they can still be dealt with by appeal, retrial, extraordinary appeal and other legal procedures.

points.text: Parties cannot object to certain lower court judgments, so a higher court should have rejected such an attempt under the cited civil and criminal procedure articles, but it wrongly overturned or sent back the judgment.
The same applies where the parties never filed an objection to the lower court's judgment but the higher court wrongly overturned it or sent it back anyway.
Both the higher court's judgment and the retrial judgment that follows are gravely contrary to law and so have no legal effect.
Because they still have the form of a judgment, they can be handled through legal procedures: by appeal if not yet final, and by retrial, extraordinary appeal or other legal procedures if final.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a husband taking a concubine gives his wife a proper reason not to live with him. The court said yes: while the husband's conduct continues, the wife has a proper reason under the Civil Code to refuse to live with him. That reason does not have to match the grounds for divorce.
raw.held: While the husband keeps a concubine, the wife's refusal to cohabit counts as a proper reason under Article 1001 of the Civil Code, and that reason need not match the divorce grounds in Article 1052. The earlier interpretation's reference to a wife requesting separation means she may refuse to cohabit, not that she may file a separation lawsuit.

points.text: The Supreme Court was unsure about an earlier interpretation (院字第七七０號 (二)), and under a prior council resolution this ruling took up the question.
Article 1001 of the Civil Code makes spouses owe each other cohabitation, unless there is a proper reason they cannot live together.

A husband taking a concubine breaches the spouses' mutual duty of fidelity, so until that conduct ends, the wife has a proper reason not to cohabit. That reason need not match the divorce grounds in Article 1052.
Because the marriage still continues, once the reason for not living together ends, the duty to cohabit applies again.
The earlier interpretation's phrase about a wife requesting separation means she may refuse cohabitation, not that she may bring a separation suit as in foreign systems.

who: Wives whose husbands take a concubine

raw.answer: The case asked whether a change to the Executive Yuan's announcement of which goods are controlled, and in what amounts, counts as a change in the law under Article 2 of the Criminal Code. The court decided it does not. So the change does not affect how smuggling committed before the change is punished.
raw.held: When the Executive Yuan changes its announcement of controlled goods and amounts under Article 2, paragraph 2 of the Smuggling Punishment Act, Article 2 of the Criminal Code does not apply to smuggling committed before the change.

points.text: Article 2 of the Criminal Code speaks of a change in the law, which means a change in the legal provisions that set the punishment.
Changing the content of the Executive Yuan's announcement is not a change to the punishment provisions of the Smuggling Punishment Act.
So such a change does not fit what Article 2 of the Criminal Code means by a change in the law, and that article does not apply.

who: People accused of smuggling before an announcement changed

raw.answer: The case asked how to count the six-month filing period for crimes that can only be prosecuted if the victim or another eligible person files a complaint, when the criminal conduct is repeated or ongoing. The court decided the period starts from when the eligible person learns of the offender's last act, or of the end of the conduct. It also changed an earlier interpretation, 院字第一二三二號.
raw.held: For such crimes, the six-month complaint period runs from when the person entitled to complain learns of the offender's last act or that the conduct has ended. The earlier interpretation 院字第一二三二號 is changed.

points.text: Counting from when the person first learns who the offender is could let the period expire while the conduct is still repeating or continuing, leaving no right to file a complaint.
The court considered that outcome contrary to reason and fairness, so the period should start from the last act or the end of the conduct.
The court's interpretations stay in effect until changed, unless they lapse because the content of the laws changed, and they must not be contradicted.

who: People entitled to file a complaint for complaint-based crimes
Offenders whose conduct is repeated or ongoing

raw.answer: The case was about how people should challenge the government's taking of farmland and its allocation to farmers under the Land-to-the-Tiller Implementation Act. The court decided that these disputes must go through administrative remedies, not civil lawsuits in ordinary courts seeking return of the land. Any contrary ordinary-court judgment cannot be enforced.
raw.held: People affected by farmland expropriation and allocation under the Act may seek relief only through administrative procedures. They may not sue in civil court to get the land back on the ground that their rights were harmed, and contrary ordinary-court judgments cannot be enforced.

points.text: Expropriating or allocating farmland under the Act is an exercise of public authority by the government.

Owners, recipients and other interested parties who think there was a mistake, whatever its kind or cause, must first apply for correction under the Act's provisions (Article 17, paragraph 1, item 2, and Article 21, item 3).

If they still disagree with the government's decision on the correction application, they must use the administrative dispute process: appeal, further appeal, and administrative litigation under Article 1 of the Administrative Appeals Act and Article 1 of the Administrative Litigation Act.
Therefore they cannot instead sue in an ordinary court, claiming harm to their rights, to demand return of the land. A contrary ordinary-court judgment cannot be enforced.

who: Other interested parties in farmland disputes

raw.answer: The case asked whether judges are bound by administrative orders that government agencies issue to explain laws and regulations. The court decided that judges should not simply set such orders aside, but they may still state their own lawful and appropriate view based on the law.
raw.held: When trying cases, judges may not directly reject and refuse to use administrative orders that agencies issue within their duties to interpret rules, but they may still express their own view, grounded in law, of what is lawful and appropriate.

points.text: Such orders may be the basis for finding facts or for deciding a case, so judges cannot directly reject and ignore them.
These orders are numerous and wide-ranging, and some may differ somewhat from the law's meaning or raise a problem under Article 172 of the Constitution, so they cannot all be treated alike.
Under Article 80 of the Constitution, judges judge independently according to the law, which is their proper duty.
Within that duty, when a point in dispute needs a correct explanation, a judge may state a lawful and appropriate view in good faith and honest conviction.

raw.answer: The case asked how a landlord or tenant can challenge a government decision on whether farmland may be taken back by the landlord for his own farming after a lease ends. The court decided that these decisions and mediations are administrative actions. People who disagree must therefore use the administrative appeal process.
raw.held: When an administrative body decides or mediates whether leased farmland can be taken back for the owner's own farming under Article 19 of the 耕地三七五減租條例, a landlord or tenant who objects must seek relief through the administrative dispute procedure.

points.text: The review and approval of whether farmland can be taken back is done by the township or district office and the county or city government under the Act's rules, so it is an administrative action.
Under Article 19, paragraph 2, the tenancy committee's mediation is a one-sided act with legal effect on a lease that has expired, so it is also an administrative action.
The mediation is issued in the name of the township or district office, which acts as an administrative body, making its administrative nature even clearer.
Article 19, paragraph 2 has no provision sending the matter to the judicial authorities, unlike Article 26, paragraph 1 of the same Act.
So objections must go through administrative appeal, a further appeal, and then an administrative lawsuit, under the 訴願法 and the 行政訴訟法.

who: Township and district offices and tenancy committees
